---
name: horizon
description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
---

You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.

## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate

Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.

You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
**shared state**, not meetings:

- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
  another team.
- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).

Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
object in `horizon inbox list --json`.

## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)

**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.

The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):

- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
  item's status/strategy current as you work. It doubles as the **project board**:
  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but

- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See

## Your session's identity (environment variables)

The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |

## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)

Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:

- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).

## One-shot discipline (important)

This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).

## Pick the highest-value work

Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.

If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
(it returns to the queue).

## Fresh-context checkpoints

The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
checkpoints:

- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
  clean/build result.

Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
terminal `done` claim.

Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.

## Warnings are work

Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that

Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When

For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its

`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake

configured final build covers the same files.

**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in

| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |

## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)

Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
needs no permission.

Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.

## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)

Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).

Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:

- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status/strategy (not a re-narration of the diff).
- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
  as **memory**.

Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.

## Resuming after an interruption

State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:

- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.

## Final report (your last message)

Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
not by itself a reason to stop.

## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)

There is no second orchestrator role running alongside you. *You* are the driver,
and the **`ground`** subagent is the scheduled fresh-context checkpoint when the
workspace or strategy needs an external view. Available helpers (see the
`subagents` skill):

- **janitor** — workspace hygiene: roadmap/READMEs concise, inbox from overflowing.
- **ground** — workspace-wide strategy, graph, ledger, and convergence review.
- **work-reviewer** — fresh-context review of your last work; is it converging?
- **blueprint** — Lean ↔ blueprint statement/`\uses` correctness for a scoped slice.
- **reference-retriever**, **debug**, **page-transcriber** — as needed.

Keep proving; delegate the upkeep.

---
name: project-git
description: How git works in an Archon Horizon workspace — one out-of-tree workspace ledger (no per-project repos); read a project's history by pathspec or by a session's commit trailers.
---

Read this before running `git diff`/`git log` on a project.

## The model

- **One out-of-tree workspace ledger.** Archon commits to a single repo whose git
  dir is `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` with the workspace **root** as its
  work tree (driven via `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`). `<root>/.git` is deliberately
  untouched — it is reserved for a user repo. The ledger records one commit per
  completed session: `config.yaml`, the session's scoped project files, and
  `.archon-horizon/` shared state; never the binary git dirs under
  `.archon-horizon/vcs/`, locks, or other volatile internals.
- **There are no per-project repositories.** A project directory has no nested
  `.git/`, and there is no `.archon-horizon/vcs/<project>.git`. A project's
  "history" is simply the workspace ledger filtered to that project's path.
- **You record your own work by committing to the ledger** with plain `git` (see
  below). Commit *early and often* with a semantic, math-first message — the
  commit message + diff is how your progress is read, so make the message say what
  you proved/built. Provenance trailers are added automatically; do not write them.

So a plain `git diff` at the root sees only a user repo (if any), never Archon's.
Drive the out-of-tree workspace ledger explicitly (or use `hgit`).

## Recording your work (committing)

Commits go to the ledger, **not** to `<root>/.git` and **not** via any project
`.git` (there is none). Do **not** `export GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` yourself — that
would redirect `lake` and other tooling. Two equivalent ways to commit:

```bash
# 1) The `hgit` wrapper (on the session env as $HORIZON_GIT) — plain git, ledger-scoped:
"$HORIZON_GIT" add path/to/File.lean
"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
  --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'

# 2) The explicit form (identical effect):
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    add path/to/File.lean
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
    --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
```

Ordinary git: the ledger's index tracks HEAD, so `add` then `commit` records your
files on top of it. Horizon's own commits stage in a private index and never leave
anything staged in your way.

- **Prefer the pathspec commit** — name the paths on the commit itself:
  `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…" --trailer 'Summary=…' -- path/to/File.lean`
  It records exactly those files, ignores whatever else may be staged, and git
  builds its tree from the **current** HEAD — so it cannot silently revert a
  concurrent session's files the way a commit built on a stale index can.
- Add at least one **`Summary` trailer** explaining the important change, not
  merely repeating the subject. Use one trailer per distinct explanation when
  useful. Its value supports Markdown and LaTeX, so concise mathematical context
  such as `--trailer 'Summary=**Invariant.** Preserves $f(x)=x$ on $A$.'` renders
  directly in the dashboard commit item. Keep each trailer on one line; repeat
  `--trailer 'Summary=…'` for a few separate points.
- Stage **explicit paths** you changed rather than `add -A` — the work tree is the
  whole workspace, so `-A` can sweep in unrelated files.
- `Archon-Run`/`Session`/`Role`/`Task`/`Projects` trailers are stamped for you by a
  hook from the session env; your message stays clean.
- Build artifacts (`.lake`, `*.olean`, …) are excluded automatically, and any
  high-confidence credential is **redacted to `XXXX`** in the staged content (not
  blocked), so a broad add still won't leak a secret into the ledger.
- If the guard reports *"redacted possible secret(s) to XXXX"*, it scrubbed a
  matched credential and let the commit through — **rotate the real credential**,
  and check you didn't stage more than you meant to (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_SECRETS=1`
  skips the scan entirely). A *separate* guard still **blocks** a commit that would
  silently delete tracked files you didn't change (a stale-index clobber); re-seed
  the index (`git read-tree HEAD && git add -- <your files>`) rather than forcing it.

Then verify **in the ledger**, and verify the **paths**, not just the SHA — a bare
`git cat-file` runs against `<root>/.git`, which has not seen your commit yet and will
make a perfectly real SHA look fabricated:

```bash
"$HORIZON_GIT" ls-tree --name-only HEAD -- path/to/File.lean   # empty ⇒ NOT in HEAD
```

## Concurrent sessions and the clobber guard

Several sessions may commit to the ledger at once. A commit whose index was
seeded from an older HEAD (e.g. `read-tree`, then a concurrent session commits,
then you commit) produces a tree that *lacks* the other session's new files —
plain git would commit it without any error and silently delete their work.
The ledger's `pre-commit` guard now rejects any commit that stages deletions
you did not ask for:

- *"this commit would DELETE N tracked file(s) you did not change"* — your
  index base is stale (or you are committing through a polluted shared index).
  **Do not override.** Re-seed and retry; your own edits are safe in the
  working tree, which concurrent commits never touch:

  ```bash
  "$HORIZON_GIT" read-tree HEAD
  "$HORIZON_GIT" add -- <your files>
  "$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…"          # or just: commit -m "…" -- <your files>
  ```

- Deleting a file **on purpose** (moved/retired): set
  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_DELETIONS=1` for that one commit.

At the **end of the session**, re-verify content — not just that HEAD moved —
since a stale-based commit elsewhere could have landed after yours (the guard
blocks new offenders, but belt-and-braces):

```bash
"$HORIZON_GIT" cat-file -e HEAD:path/to/File.lean && \
"$HORIZON_GIT" show HEAD:path/to/File.lean | diff -q - path/to/File.lean
```

If you were clobbered anyway: `read-tree HEAD`, re-add your files from the
working tree, commit once.

## Reading history / a project's diff

Run from the workspace root:

```bash
GD=.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git

git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20                       # whole ledger
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20 -- <project-path>     # one project
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- <project-path>
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- '<project-path>/*.lean'
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. show <sha>
```

Each commit carries provenance trailers — `Archon-Run`, `Archon-Session`,
`Archon-Role`, `Archon-Task`, `Archon-Projects` — so you can map a commit to the
run/session that made it and see what it touched without parsing prose:

```bash
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. \
  log --format='%H %(trailers:key=Archon-Session,valueonly)' -- <project-path>
```

To see what the previous Horizon agent changed, find its session's commit(s) by
the `Archon-Session` trailer and diff each against **its own parent** (what that
commit changed).

9	/-!
10	# The symmetric power is a colimit of the permutation action
11	
12	`Albanese/SymPowInterface.lean` names the universal property of `Sym^n C` as data
13	(`SymPowData`) and proves Milne's Albanese argument over it. It also records the honest
14	limitation: the *bare* structure is trivially inhabited (`symPowDataTrivial`, take
15	`proj := 𝟙`), so what the downstream theorems quantify over is the **pair**
16	`(D, hproj)` with `hproj : ∀ σ, permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj`, and that pair had only
17	one witness — `n = 1`.
18	
19	This file removes that limitation by identifying what the pair *is*.
20	
21	## The identification
22	
23	Let `permDiagram C n : SingleObj (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ⥤ K` be the one-object diagram of
24	the `S_n`-action on `C^n` by `permAut`. Then:
25	
26	* `symPowOfColimit` — a colimit of `permDiagram C n` **is** a `SymPowData C n`, and
27	* `symPowOfColimit_proj_perm` — its projection is symmetric **for free**: the symmetry
28	  hypothesis is literally `colimit.w`, the cocone condition;
29	* `SymPowData.isColimit` — conversely, any pair `(D, hproj)` *is* a colimit of the same
30	  diagram.
31	
32	So the pair the Albanese theorems consume is not merely *implied by* a quotient — it is
33	**equivalent** to a colimit of the permutation action. That is the categorical content of
34	Milne III.3 Proposition 3.1 separated from its affine-and-glue implementation.
35	
36	## Why this is a reduction and not a restatement
37	
38	Three things change, and each is checked below rather than asserted.
39	
40	1. **The trivial witness is refuted, in the tree.** `permAut_swap_ne_id` exhibits a
41	   concrete `K` (`Type`), a concrete object (`Bool`) and `n = 2` at which
42	   `permAut ≠ 𝟙`; hence `symPowDataTrivial` genuinely fails `hproj` there
43	   (`symPowDataTrivial_not_proj_perm`). The `SymPowInterface` header asserted this;
44	   nothing had checked it.
45	2. **The pair is inhabited at every `n`, not just `n = 1`**, in any cartesian monoidal
46	   category with the relevant colimit — `symPowData_of_hasColimit`. The interface's
47	   `n = 1`-only caveat was a statement about `K`, not about `n`.
48	3. **The obligation becomes a mathlib-shaped one.** "Construct `Sym^n C`" is replaced by
49	   `HasColimit (permDiagram C n)`. For the two categories checked here — `Type u` and
50	   affine `k`-schemes `(Under k)ᵒᵖ` — mathlib *already* discharges it, so the pair is
51	   inhabited there at every `n` with no new geometry (`symPowDataType`,
52	   `symPowDataAffine`).
53	
54	## What is still open, stated precisely
55	
56	`Sym^n C` for `C` a **proper** curve in `Over (Spec k̄)`. `Over (Spec k̄)` is not known to
57	have these colimits: the affine construction glues, and gluing is exactly the part of
58	Milne III.3.1 that this file does not do. The gain is not that the curve case is done —
59	it is that the remaining obligation is now one named instance about one named diagram,
60	the symmetry half is discharged permanently, and the affine case is *proved* rather than
61	scoped at hundreds of lines.
62	
63	Note also the direction of the equivalence: because `SymPowData.isColimit` shows the pair
64	*is* a colimit, no future construction can supply the pair without supplying that colimit.
65	The reduction is therefore lossless — it cannot have replaced the problem with a
66	strictly harder one.
67	
68	## References
69	
70	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §III.3 Proposition 3.1 (the symmetric power), p. 94; §III.6
71	Proposition 6.1, p. 104. Blueprint `def:symmetric_power_curve`. The consumer is
72	`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`.
73	-/
74	
75	set_option autoImplicit false
76	
77	universe v u
78	
79	open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory
80	
81	namespace CategoryTheory
82	
83	variable {K : Type u} [Category.{v} K] [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] [HasFiniteProducts K]
84	
85	/-! ## §1. The permutation action as a diagram
86	
87	`MonObj.permAut` (`Albanese/GrpObjFoldSum.lean`) gives the factor-permuting endomorphism
88	of `C^n`. Bundling it as a monoid homomorphism into `End (C^n)` turns the `S_n`-action
89	into a functor out of `SingleObj (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, which is the shape mathlib's
90	colimit API consumes.
91	
92	One convention point worth stating, since it is the only place a sign can go wrong:
93	composition in `End X` is `f * g = g ≫ f`, so a *homomorphism* out of `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`
94	must use `σ ↦ permAut C σ⁻¹`. With that inverse the multiplicativity is `rfl` after
95	projecting; without it one gets an anti-homomorphism. -/
96	
97	/-- **The `S_n`-action on `C^n`, as a monoid homomorphism into `End (C^n)`.**
98	
99	Sends `σ` to `permAut C σ⁻¹`. The inverse is forced by mathlib's `End` convention
100	(`f * g = g ≫ f`); see the section note. -/
101	noncomputable def permEnd (C : K) (n : ℕ) :
102	    Equiv.Perm (Fin n) →* End (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) where
103	  toFun σ := MonObj.permAut C σ⁻¹
104	  map_one' := by
105	    apply Pi.hom_ext; intro i
106	    rw [MonObj.permAut_π]; simp
107	  map_mul' σ τ := by
108	    apply Pi.hom_ext; intro i
109	    change MonObj.permAut C (σ * τ)⁻¹ ≫ _ = (MonObj.permAut C τ⁻¹ ≫ MonObj.permAut C σ⁻¹) ≫ _
110	    rw [MonObj.permAut_π, Category.assoc, MonObj.permAut_π, MonObj.permAut_π]
111	    rfl
112	
113	/-- **The permutation-action diagram.** The one-object diagram in `K` whose single value
114	is `C^n` and whose endomorphisms are the factor permutations. A colimit of it is the
115	quotient `C^n / S_n`. -/
116	noncomputable def permDiagram (C : K) (n : ℕ) : SingleObj (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ⥤ K :=
117	  SingleObj.functor (permEnd C n)
118	
119	variable (C : K) (n : ℕ)
120	
121	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
122	/-- The diagram's value at the unique object is `C^n`. -/
123	theorem permDiagram_obj (j : SingleObj (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))) :
124	    (permDiagram C n).obj j = ∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C) := rfl
125	
126	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
127	/-- **The action, expressed as a diagram map.** `permAut C σ` is the diagram's map at
128	`σ⁻¹`; the double inverse is the `End`-convention bookkeeping of `permEnd`. This is the
129	bridge every proof below crosses. -/
130	theorem permAut_eq_map (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
131	    MonObj.permAut C σ = (permDiagram C n).map (SingleObj.toEnd (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) σ⁻¹) := by
132	  change MonObj.permAut C σ = MonObj.permAut C σ⁻¹⁻¹
133	  rw [inv_inv]
134	
135	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
136	/-- **Every cocone leg is symmetric.** This is the cocone condition `Cocone.w` read
137	through `permAut_eq_map`, and it is the reason the symmetry hypothesis of `SymPowData`
138	costs nothing on the colimit side. -/
139	theorem cocone_app_perm (c : Cocone (permDiagram C n)) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
140	    MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ c.ι.app (SingleObj.star _) = c.ι.app (SingleObj.star _) := by
141	  rw [permAut_eq_map C n σ]
142	  exact c.w (SingleObj.toEnd (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) σ⁻¹)
143	
144	/-- **A symmetric morphism out of `C^n` is a cocone.** The converse packaging of
145	`cocone_app_perm`: `S_n`-invariance of `h` is exactly the cocone condition. -/
146	noncomputable def symCocone {T : K} (h : (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ T)
147	    (hsym : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ h = h) :
148	    Cocone (permDiagram C n) where
149	  pt := T
150	  ι :=
151	    { app := fun _ => h
152	      naturality := by
153	        intro X Y f
154	        change MonObj.permAut C (f : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))⁻¹ ≫ h = h ≫ 𝟙 T
155	        rw [Category.comp_id]
156	        exact hsym _ }
157	
158	/-! ## §2. A colimit of the action is a `SymPowData`, with symmetry for free
159	
160	This is the forward half of the identification. Note which part is doing the work: the
161	universal property of `SymPowData` is `colimit.desc` plus `colimit.hom_ext`, and the
162	symmetry hypothesis `hproj` — the half that ruled out the trivial witness and had only
163	an `n = 1` witness before — is `colimit.w`. Nothing is assumed about `n`. -/
164	
165	section OfColimit
166	
167	variable [HasColimit (permDiagram C n)]
168	
169	/-- **The symmetric power from a colimit of the permutation action.**
170	
171	`carrier := colimit (permDiagram C n)`, `proj := colimit.ι`, and the universal property is
172	`colimit.desc` — a symmetric `h` is a cocone by `symCocone`, and uniqueness is
173	`colimit.hom_ext` on the one-object index category. -/
174	noncomputable def symPowOfColimit : SymPowData C n where
175	  carrier := colimit (permDiagram C n)
176	  proj := colimit.ι (permDiagram C n) (SingleObj.star _)
177	  desc := fun {T} h hsym => by
178	    have hd : colimit.ι (permDiagram C n) (SingleObj.star _)
179	        ≫ colimit.desc (permDiagram C n) (symCocone C n h hsym) = h :=
180	      colimit.ι_desc (symCocone C n h hsym) (SingleObj.star _)
181	    refine ⟨colimit.desc (permDiagram C n) (symCocone C n h hsym), hd, ?_⟩
182	    intro u hu
183	    exact colimit.hom_ext fun j => by
184	      obtain rfl : j = SingleObj.star _ := Subsingleton.elim _ _
185	      exact hu.trans hd.symm
186	
187	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
188	@[simp]
189	theorem symPowOfColimit_carrier :
190	    (symPowOfColimit C n).carrier = colimit (permDiagram C n) := rfl
191	
192	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
193	@[simp]
194	theorem symPowOfColimit_proj :
195	    (symPowOfColimit C n).proj = colimit.ι (permDiagram C n) (SingleObj.star _) := rfl
196	
197	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
198	/-- **The symmetry hypothesis, for free.** The projection of `symPowOfColimit` is
199	`S_n`-symmetric because that is the cocone condition `colimit.w`.
200	
201	This is the declaration that changes the interface's status: `SymPowInterface.lean` needs
202	the *pair* `(D, hproj)`, and here `hproj` comes with the object at no cost and at every
203	`n`. -/
204	theorem symPowOfColimit_proj_perm (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
205	    MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ (symPowOfColimit C n).proj = (symPowOfColimit C n).proj := by
206	  have h := colimit.w (permDiagram C n) (SingleObj.toEnd (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) σ⁻¹)
207	  change MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ colimit.ι (permDiagram C n) (SingleObj.star _) = _
208	  rw [permAut_eq_map C n σ]
209	  exact h
210	
211	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
212	/-- **The pair, packaged.** Existence of the object the Albanese theorems quantify over,
213	in the form a call site consumes: a `SymPowData` *together with* its symmetry. -/
214	theorem symPowData_of_hasColimit :
215	    ∃ D : SymPowData C n, ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n),
216	      MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj :=
217	  ⟨symPowOfColimit C n, symPowOfColimit_proj_perm C n⟩
218	
219	end OfColimit
220	
221	/-! ## §3. Conversely: the pair *is* a colimit
222	
223	The other half of the identification, and the one that makes the reduction lossless. Any
224	`SymPowData` whose projection is symmetric exhibits its carrier as a colimit of
225	`permDiagram C n`.
226	
227	Consequence worth stating explicitly, because it is what rules out having traded the
228	problem for a harder one: nobody can supply the pair `(D, hproj)` *without* supplying this
229	colimit. So `HasColimit (permDiagram C n)` is not a sufficient condition that might be
230	stronger than needed — it is equivalent to the thing the Albanese argument consumes. -/
231	
232	section ToColimit
233	
234	/-- The cocone attached to a `SymPowData` with symmetric projection. -/
235	noncomputable def SymPowData.cocone (D : SymPowData C n)
236	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj) :
237	    Cocone (permDiagram C n) where
238	  pt := D.carrier
239	  ι :=
240	    { app := fun _ => D.proj
241	      naturality := by
242	        intro X Y f
243	        change MonObj.permAut C (f : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))⁻¹ ≫ D.proj = D.proj ≫ 𝟙 _
244	        rw [Category.comp_id]
245	        exact hproj _ }
246	
247	/-- **The pair is a colimit.** A `SymPowData` with symmetric projection is precisely a
248	colimit of the permutation action — its universal property *is* the colimit property,
249	transported across the fact that a cocone on a one-object diagram is a symmetric
250	morphism (`cocone_app_perm`). -/
251	noncomputable def SymPowData.isColimit (D : SymPowData C n)
252	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj) :
253	    IsColimit (D.cocone C n hproj) where
254	  desc c := (D.desc (c.ι.app (SingleObj.star _)) (cocone_app_perm C n c)).choose
255	  fac c j := by
256	    obtain rfl : j = SingleObj.star _ := Subsingleton.elim _ _
257	    exact (D.desc (c.ι.app (SingleObj.star _)) (cocone_app_perm C n c)).choose_spec.1
258	  uniq c u hu :=
259	    (D.desc (c.ι.app (SingleObj.star _)) (cocone_app_perm C n c)).choose_spec.2 u
260	      (hu (SingleObj.star _))
261	
262	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
263	/-- **The obligation is exactly a `HasColimit`.** Supplying the pair the Albanese
264	theorems quantify over is equivalent to the diagram having a colimit — so replacing
265	"construct `Sym^n C`" by `HasColimit (permDiagram C n)` neither weakens nor strengthens
266	the problem. -/
267	theorem hasColimit_permDiagram_iff :
268	    HasColimit (permDiagram C n) ↔
269	      ∃ D : SymPowData C n, ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n),
270	        MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj := by
271	  refine ⟨fun _ => symPowData_of_hasColimit C n, fun ⟨D, hproj⟩ => ?_⟩
272	  exact ⟨⟨⟨D.cocone C n hproj, D.isColimit C n hproj⟩⟩⟩
273	
274	end ToColimit
275	
276	end CategoryTheory

278	/-! ## §4. The trivial witness is genuinely refuted at `n = 2`
279	
280	`SymPowInterface.lean` keeps `symPowDataTrivial` (`proj := 𝟙`) as its acceptance test and
281	states that it fails the symmetry hypothesis for `n ≥ 2` "since it would force
282	`permAut C σ = 𝟙`". That was an *assertion*: nothing in the tree had exhibited a category
283	and an object where `permAut` at a transposition really differs from the identity, so the
284	argument for why the interface is not vacuous rested on an unchecked step.
285	
286	It is checked here, concretely: `K = Type`, `C = Bool`, `n = 2`, `σ = swap 0 1`. Evaluating
287	both projections at the tuple `(true, false)` separates them. -/
288	
289	namespace CategoryTheory
290	
291	open Limits
292	
293	/-- The tuple `(true, false)` in `Bool²`, as a `Type`-morphism out of `Bool`. Used only to
294	separate the two projections. -/
295	noncomputable def boolPairTuple : (Bool : Type) ⟶ (∏ᶜ fun _ : Fin 2 => (Bool : Type)) :=
296	  Pi.lift (P := (Bool : Type))
297	    (fun i : Fin 2 => TypeCat.ofHom (fun _ : Bool => decide (i = 0)))
298	
299	/-- **`permAut` at a transposition is not the identity.** Witnessed in `Type` at `Bool`
300	and `n = 2`: composing with the `0`-th projection turns `permAut (swap 0 1) = 𝟙` into
301	`π₁ = π₀`, which the tuple `(true, false)` refutes.
302	
303	This is the fact that makes `SymPowData`'s symmetry hypothesis non-vacuous for `n ≥ 2`. -/
304	theorem permAut_swap_ne_id :
305	    MonObj.permAut (Bool : Type) (Equiv.swap (0 : Fin 2) 1) ≠ 𝟙 _ := by
306	  intro hc
307	  have h0 := congrArg (fun f => f ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 2 => (Bool : Type)) 0) hc
308	  simp only [MonObj.permAut_π, Category.id_comp] at h0
309	  rw [Equiv.swap_apply_left] at h0
310	  have h1 := congrArg (fun f => boolPairTuple ≫ f) h0
311	  simp only [boolPairTuple, Pi.lift_π] at h1
312	  have h2 := congrArg
313	    (fun (f : (Bool : Type) ⟶ (Bool : Type)) => ConcreteCategory.hom f true) h1
314	  simp at h2
315	
316	/-- **The trivial datum fails the symmetry hypothesis.** So `symPowDataTrivial` is not a
317	witness for the pair `(D, hproj)` at `n = 2`, and the `SymPowInterface` header's
318	contrastive claim is now a checked fact rather than a remark. -/
319	theorem symPowDataTrivial_not_proj_perm :
320	    ¬ (∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin 2),
321	        MonObj.permAut (Bool : Type) σ ≫ (symPowDataTrivial (Bool : Type) 2).proj
322	          = (symPowDataTrivial (Bool : Type) 2).proj) := by
323	  intro h
324	  refine permAut_swap_ne_id ?_
325	  have h2 := h (Equiv.swap 0 1)
326	  change MonObj.permAut (Bool : Type) (Equiv.swap 0 1) ≫ 𝟙 _ = 𝟙 _ at h2
327	  rwa [Category.comp_id] at h2
328	
329	end CategoryTheory
330	
331	/-! ## §5. Where mathlib already discharges the obligation
332	
333	Two categories where `HasColimit (permDiagram C n)` is available with no new geometry, so
334	the pair `(D, hproj)` is inhabited **at every `n`**:
335	
336	* `Type u` — colimits of every shape;
337	* affine `k`-schemes, presented as `(Under k)ᵒᵖ`. This is the affine case of Milne III.3
338	  Proposition 3.1: dually the colimit is `Spec` of the ring of `S_n`-invariants of the
339	  `n`-fold tensor power, which is exactly Milne's `Spec (A^{⊗n})^{S_n}`. Mathlib supplies
340	  it through limits in `Under k`, so the affine half of that proposition needs no
341	  construction here.
342	
343	What is *not* here is the curve case: `Over (Spec k̄)` with `C` proper. The gluing of the
344	affine quotients — the remaining half of Milne III.3.1 — is what would give that, and it
345	is the honest boundary. -/

347	namespace CategoryTheory
348	
349	open Limits
350	
351	/-- **A one-object diagram's sections are its invariants.** For a diagram indexed by
352	`SingleObj G`, lying in the `sections` set is equivalent to being fixed by every `g : G` —
353	the many-object quantifier collapses because the index category has one object and
354	`SingleObj.toEnd` is an equivalence onto its endomorphisms.
355	
356	This is what makes the affine case below *computable* rather than merely abstract. Limits
357	in `CommRingCat` are computed as sections (`CommRingCat.limitCone`), so dually the colimit
358	of the permutation action on an affine scheme is `Spec` of the **invariant subring** of the
359	`n`-fold tensor power — which is exactly the ring Milne writes as `(A^{⊗n})^{S_n}` in
360	III.3 Proposition 3.1. Without this the affine inhabitation would be a black box; with it,
361	the carrier is named. -/
362	theorem mem_sections_singleObj_iff {G : Type u} [Group G] (F : SingleObj G ⥤ Type v)
363	    (x : (j : SingleObj G) → F.obj j) :
364	    x ∈ F.sections ↔
365	      ∀ g : G, F.map (SingleObj.toEnd G g) (x (SingleObj.star G)) = x (SingleObj.star G) := by
366	  refine ⟨fun hx g => hx (SingleObj.toEnd G g), fun h j j' f => ?_⟩
367	  obtain rfl : j = SingleObj.star G := Subsingleton.elim _ _
368	  obtain rfl : j' = SingleObj.star G := Subsingleton.elim _ _
369	  exact h ((SingleObj.toEnd G).symm f)
370	
371	/-- **Every `n`, in `Type`.** The symmetric power interface with its symmetry hypothesis,
372	inhabited at all `n` — `Type` has all colimits.
373	
374	Contrast with `symPowDataOne`: that was `n = 1` only. Here `n` is arbitrary, so the
375	statements the Albanese argument quantifies over are non-vacuous in the range where the
376	group-law step is genuinely exercised. -/
377	theorem symPowData_type (X : Type u) (n : ℕ) :
378	    ∃ D : SymPowData X n, ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n),
379	      MonObj.permAut X σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj :=
380	  symPowData_of_hasColimit X n
381	
382	/-- **Every `n`, for affine `k`-schemes** — the affine case of Milne III.3 Proposition 3.1.
383	
384	`(Under k)ᵒᵖ` is the category of affine `k`-schemes; its colimits are limits in
385	`Under k`, and dually the colimit of the permutation action on the `n`-fold coproduct is
386	`Spec` of the invariant subring of the `n`-fold tensor power. Mathlib has both, so this
387	holds with no construction. -/
388	theorem symPowData_affine (k : CommRingCat.{u}) (X : (Under k)ᵒᵖ) (n : ℕ) :
389	    letI : CartesianMonoidalCategory (Under k)ᵒᵖ := ofHasFiniteProducts
390	    ∃ D : SymPowData X n, ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n),
391	      MonObj.permAut X σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj :=
392	  letI : CartesianMonoidalCategory (Under k)ᵒᵖ := ofHasFiniteProducts
393	  symPowData_of_hasColimit X n
394	
395	end CategoryTheory

411	hypotheses in sight. Which is the right shape for it: it is a general fact about schemes

9	/-!
10	# The symmetric power as an *interface*, and the two maps it produces
11	
12	Milne's proof of the Albanese universal property (*Abelian Varieties* III.6
13	Proposition 6.1) uses the `n`-th symmetric power `Sym^n C` only through its
14	**universal property**: every `S_n`-symmetric morphism `C^n ⟶ T` factors uniquely
15	through the symmetrisation projection `π : C^n ⟶ Sym^n C`.
16	
17	At this Mathlib pin the *object* `Sym^n C` does not exist — there is no quotient of
18	a scheme by a finite group action (`analogies/m3-route-audit.md` sizes the
19	construction at roughly 2400–3800 lines, and mathlib's `SymmetricPower` is for
20	modules). Writing `Sym^n C := sorry` makes every downstream equation a statement
21	about a junk term, which is why `Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean` keeps its obligations
22	unproved rather than discharging them against a meaningless definition.
23	
24	This file takes the other route: it **names the interface** as a structure
25	`SymPowData C n`, and then proves, unconditionally, everything Milne's argument
26	derives from it. The missing geometry is isolated in exactly one place — inhabiting
27	`SymPowData` — and nothing downstream is a statement about `sorry`.
28	
29	## What is proved here (no `sorry`, nothing conditional on unproved statements)
30	
31	* `SymPowData.symAVMap` — Milne's `Sym^n φ`. Given `φ : C ⟶ A` into a *commutative*
32	  monoid object, the `n`-fold sum `powSum n φ` is `S_n`-symmetric
33	  (`MonObj.powSum_perm`, already proved), so the interface descends it. This is the
34	  content of `lem:symmetric_product_av_map`, and it is a construction, not a
35	  hypothesis.
36	* `SymPowData.proj_comp_symAVMap` / `SymPowData.symAVMap_unique` — its defining
37	  equation and uniqueness.
38	* `MonObj.basePointShift` — the morphism `Q ↦ (P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)` placing `Q` in a
39	  designated slot `i₀` and the basepoint elsewhere. Milne's `Q ↦ Q + (n−1) P₀`
40	  factors through it.
41	* `MonObj.basePointShift_comp_powSum` — **the computation that makes the backward
42	  direction of the Albanese connector work**: for a *pointed* `φ` (`P₀ ≫ φ = η[A]`),
43	
44	  `basePointShift P₀ i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ`,
45	
46	  because `φ(Q) + φ(P₀) + ⋯ + φ(P₀) = φ(Q) + η + ⋯ + η = φ(Q)`. In the hom-monoid
47	  this is `Finset.prod_ite_eq`; the geometry evaporates exactly as it does in
48	  `GrpObjFoldSum.lean`.
49	* `symPowDataOne` and `symPowDataOne_proj_perm` — **an inhabitant of the interface
50	  *together with* the symmetry hypothesis**: `Sym^1 C = C`. See the warning below for
51	  why both halves are needed and what they do and do not show.
52	
53	## What non-vacuity does and does not mean here — read this before citing it
54	
55	`SymPowData C n` **on its own is trivially inhabited for every `n`** — and the witness
56	is recorded below as `symPowDataTrivial` rather than left as a remark, so that nobody
57	has to rediscover it:
58	
59	```
60	carrier := C^n,  proj := 𝟙,  desc := fun h _ => ⟨h, Category.id_comp h, …⟩
61	```
62	
63	With `proj = 𝟙` the universal property degenerates to `∃! u, 𝟙 ≫ u = h`. So the bare
64	structure is nearly free, and exhibiting *some* `SymPowData` proves nothing.
65	
66	What the downstream theorems actually quantify over is the **pair**
67	`(D, hproj)`, where `hproj : ∀ σ, permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj` says the projection
68	is genuinely symmetric. The `proj := 𝟙` trick fails that for `n ≥ 2` (it would need
69	`permAut C σ = 𝟙`). So the pair is the meaningful object, and this file witnesses it
70	for `n = 1`: `symPowDataOne` plus `symPowDataOne_proj_perm`.
71	
72	Two honest caveats about that witness:
73	
74	* `n = 1` is the case where the *interesting* step degenerates. The forward direction
75	  of the connector (`Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean`) uses that `ψ` is a homomorphism
76	  to move it through a `g`-fold product; a 1-fold product has one factor, so at
77	  `n = 1` that step is mere associativity. The general-`n` theorem is the real one —
78	  do not cite `n = 1` as evidence that the group law is exercised.
79	* Consequently, "the interface is inhabited" should be read as *the hypotheses are
80	  consistent and the statements are not about nothing*, not as *the hard case is
81	  covered*.
82	
83	## What is *not* here
84	
85	`SymPowData C n` for `n ≥ 2`. That is the missing quotient, and it is the honest
86	boundary of this leg. See `Albanese/AlbaneseFromData.lean` for the Albanese
87	universal property proved over this interface, and the header of
88	`Albanese/AlbaneseUP.lean` for the pinned statements.
89	
90	## References
91	
92	Milne, *Abelian Varieties*, §III.3 Proposition 3.1 (the symmetric power) and §III.6
93	Proposition 6.1, p. 104; blueprint `def:symmetric_power_curve` and
94	`lem:symmetric_product_av_map` in `blueprint/src/chapters/Albanese_AlbaneseUP.tex`.
95	-/

101	open CategoryTheory Limits MonoidalCategory CartesianMonoidalCategory
102	
103	namespace CategoryTheory
104	
105	variable {K : Type u} [Category.{v} K] [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] [HasFiniteProducts K]

107	/-! ## §1. The interface
108	
109	`SymPowData C n` is exactly the data Milne's proof uses: a scheme, a symmetrisation
110	projection from `C^n`, and the universal property for `S_n`-symmetric morphisms. The
111	symmetry hypothesis is phrased with `MonObj.permAut` (`Albanese/GrpObjFoldSum.lean`),
112	the factor-permuting automorphism of `C^n`. -/
113	
114	/-- **The universal property of the `n`-th symmetric power, as data.**
115	
116	A `SymPowData C n` is a `carrier` (morally `Sym^n C`) together with a symmetrisation
117	morphism `proj : C^n ⟶ carrier` through which *every* `S_n`-symmetric morphism out of
118	`C^n` factors uniquely.
119	
120	This is the interface, not the construction: see `symPowDataOne` for the case `n = 1`,
121	and the module header for why the general case is a separate subproject. -/
122	structure SymPowData (C : K) (n : ℕ) where
123	  /-- The underlying object, morally `Sym^n C`. -/
124	  carrier : K
125	  /-- The symmetrisation projection `π : C^n ⟶ Sym^n C`. -/
126	  proj : (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ carrier
127	  /-- **The universal property.** Every `S_n`-symmetric morphism `C^n ⟶ T` factors
128	  uniquely through `proj`. -/
129	  desc : ∀ {T : K} (h : (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ T),
130	    (∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ h = h) →
131	    ∃! u : carrier ⟶ T, proj ≫ u = h
132	
133	namespace SymPowData
134	
135	variable {C : K} {n : ℕ}
136	
137	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
138	/-- Uniqueness of a factorisation through `proj`, in the form used at call sites:
139	two morphisms out of the carrier that agree after `proj` are equal.
140	
141	Note that no symmetry hypothesis is needed: if `u₁` and `u₂` both factor `h` then
142	`h` *is* symmetric (being `proj ≫ u₁` with `proj` symmetric would be the argument,
143	but here we get it more cheaply — apply `desc` to `proj ≫ u₁`, whose symmetry follows
144	from that of `proj` composed with anything). We therefore take the symmetry of
145	`proj` itself as the input. -/
146	theorem hom_ext_of_proj (D : SymPowData C n) {T : K} {u₁ u₂ : D.carrier ⟶ T}
147	    (hproj : ∀ σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n), MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj)
148	    (h : D.proj ≫ u₁ = D.proj ≫ u₂) : u₁ = u₂ := by
149	  obtain ⟨u, -, huniq⟩ := D.desc (D.proj ≫ u₁) (fun σ => by rw [← Category.assoc, hproj])
150	  rw [huniq u₁ rfl, huniq u₂ h.symm]
151	
152	section SymAVMap
153	
154	variable [BraidedCategory K]
155	
156	/-- **Milne's `Sym^n φ`.** For `φ : C ⟶ A` into a commutative monoid object, the
157	`n`-fold sum `(P₁,…,P_n) ↦ φ(P₁) + ⋯ + φ(P_n)` is `S_n`-symmetric
158	(`MonObj.powSum_perm` — Milne's "clearly this is symmetric"), so the interface
159	descends it to `Sym^n C ⟶ A`.
160	
161	This is `lem:symmetric_product_av_map`: a *construction* from the interface, with no
162	further geometric input. -/
163	noncomputable def symAVMap {A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
164	    (D : SymPowData C n) (φ : C ⟶ A) : D.carrier ⟶ A :=
165	  (D.desc (MonObj.powSum n φ) (fun σ => MonObj.powSum_perm n φ σ)).choose
166	
167	/-- The defining equation of `Sym^n φ`: it restores the `n`-fold sum along `proj`. -/
168	@[reassoc]
169	theorem proj_comp_symAVMap {A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
170	    (D : SymPowData C n) (φ : C ⟶ A) :
171	    D.proj ≫ D.symAVMap φ = MonObj.powSum n φ :=
172	  (D.desc (MonObj.powSum n φ) (fun σ => MonObj.powSum_perm n φ σ)).choose_spec.1
173	
174	/-- `Sym^n φ` is the *unique* morphism restoring the `n`-fold sum along `proj`. -/
175	theorem symAVMap_unique {A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
176	    (D : SymPowData C n) (φ : C ⟶ A) (u : D.carrier ⟶ A)
177	    (hu : D.proj ≫ u = MonObj.powSum n φ) : u = D.symAVMap φ :=
178	  (D.desc (MonObj.powSum n φ) (fun σ => MonObj.powSum_perm n φ σ)).choose_spec.2 u hu
179	
180	end SymAVMap
181	
182	end SymPowData

184	/-! ## §2. Milne's `Q ↦ Q + (n − 1) P₀`, and why it collapses the sum
185	
186	The backward direction of the Albanese connector restricts the symmetric-power
187	equation along `Q ↦ (Q, P₀, …, P₀)`. The whole force of that step is the following
188	computation in the hom-monoid: summing `φ` over such a tuple gives
189	`φ(Q) + φ(P₀) + ⋯ + φ(P₀)`, and a *pointed* `φ` kills every term but the first. -/
190	
191	namespace MonObj
192	
193	variable {C : K}
194	
195	/-- **The basepoint shift `Q ↦ (P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)`**, placing `Q` in the designated
196	slot `i₀` and the basepoint `P₀ : 𝟙_ ⟶ C` in every other slot.
197	
198	Composed with the symmetrisation projection this is Milne's
199	`Q ↦ Q + (n − 1) P₀ : C ⟶ Sym^n C`. -/
200	noncomputable def basePointShift (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ : Fin n) :
201	    C ⟶ (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) :=
202	  Pi.lift (fun i => if i = i₀ then 𝟙 C else toUnit C ≫ P0)
203	
204	@[reassoc (attr := simp)]
205	theorem basePointShift_π (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ i : Fin n) :
206	    basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i
207	      = if i = i₀ then 𝟙 C else toUnit C ≫ P0 := by
208	  simp only [basePointShift, Pi.lift_π]
209	
210	section Collapse
211	
212	variable [BraidedCategory K]
213	
214	/-- **The collapse computation.** For `φ : C ⟶ A` into a commutative monoid object
215	which is *pointed* at `P₀` (`P₀ ≫ φ = η[A]`), summing `φ` over the tuple
216	`(P₀, …, Q, …, P₀)` returns `φ` itself:
217	
218	`basePointShift P₀ i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ`.
219	
220	Every slot other than `i₀` contributes `toUnit ≫ P₀ ≫ φ = toUnit ≫ η[A] = 1`, the
221	identity of the hom-monoid, so the product collapses to the single factor at `i₀`
222	(`Finset.prod_ite_eq`). This is the entire content of Milne's "restrict along
223	`Q ↦ Q + (g − 1) P₀` and use `φ(P₀) = η_A`". -/
224	theorem basePointShift_comp_powSum {A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A]
225	    (P0 : 𝟙_ K ⟶ C) {n : ℕ} (i₀ : Fin n) (φ : C ⟶ A) (hφ : P0 ≫ φ = η[A]) :
226	    basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ powSum n φ = φ := by
227	  classical
228	  rw [comp_powSum]
229	  have hterm : ∀ i : Fin n,
230	      basePointShift P0 i₀ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ
231	        = if i₀ = i then φ else 1 := by
232	    intro i
233	    rw [← Category.assoc, basePointShift_π]
234	    by_cases h : i = i₀
235	    · subst h; simp
236	    · rw [if_neg h, if_neg (fun hc => h hc.symm), Category.assoc, hφ, ← Hom.one_def]
237	  rw [Finset.prod_congr rfl (fun i _ => hterm i), Finset.prod_ite_eq]
238	  simp
239	
240	end Collapse
241	
242	end MonObj

244	/-! ## §3. The interface is inhabited: `Sym^1 C = C`
245	
246	For `n = 1` the symmetric group is trivial, `C^1 ⟶ C` is an isomorphism, and the
247	universal property is immediate. Both halves of the meaningful object are supplied: the
248	datum `symPowDataOne` and the symmetry `symPowDataOne_proj_perm`.
249	
250	As the module header warns, the bare structure `SymPowData C n` is trivially inhabited
251	for every `n` (take `proj := 𝟙`), so it is the **pair** with `hproj` that carries
252	content — and `n = 1` is the degenerate case for the group-law step. See the header. -/
253	
254	/-- **`Sym^1 C = C`.** The unique projection `C^1 ⟶ C` is an isomorphism, so every
255	morphism out of `C^1` — symmetric or not, since `S_1` is trivial — factors uniquely
256	through it.
257	
258	For `n ≥ 2` inhabiting `SymPowData` *together with the symmetry hypothesis* is the
259	missing scheme-quotient construction. -/
260	noncomputable def symPowDataOne (C : K) : SymPowData C 1 where
261	  carrier := C
262	  proj := Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0
263	  desc := fun {T} h _ => by
264	    -- `Pi.lift (fun _ => 𝟙 C)` is a two-sided inverse of the single projection.
265	    have hsec : Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 = 𝟙 C := by
266	      rw [Pi.lift_π]
267	    have hret : Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 ≫ Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C))
268	        = 𝟙 (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin 1 => C)) := by
269	      apply Pi.hom_ext
270	      intro b
271	      have hb : b = 0 := Subsingleton.elim _ _
272	      subst hb
273	      rw [Category.assoc, Pi.lift_π, Category.comp_id, Category.id_comp]
274	    refine ⟨Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ h, ?_, ?_⟩
275	    · change Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 ≫ Pi.lift (fun _ : Fin 1 => (𝟙 C)) ≫ h = h
276	      rw [← Category.assoc, hret, Category.id_comp]
277	    · intro u hu
278	      rw [← hu, ← Category.assoc, hsec, Category.id_comp]
279	
280	/-- **The trivial witness — kept deliberately, as the acceptance test for this file.**
281	
282	`SymPowData C n` is inhabited for *every* `n` by taking `proj := 𝟙`, which makes the
283	universal property vacuous. This declaration exists so that the limitation is a checked
284	fact in the tree rather than a remark someone might doubt or forget.
285	
286	Its purpose is contrastive: a downstream theorem is only meaningful because it *also*
287	requires `hproj : ∀ σ, permAut C σ ≫ D.proj = D.proj`, which this datum **fails** for
288	`n ≥ 2` (it would force `permAut C σ = 𝟙`). Do not use it for anything; if a future
289	lemma over `SymPowData` can be instantiated at `symPowDataTrivial`, that lemma is
290	vacuous and the bug is in the lemma.
291	
292	(The general lesson, arrived at independently in the `ajc-pic0av` lane the same day for
293	`PicScheme.ClassDegree`: an interface reduces something only when it asserts a
294	*nontrivial* property, and the test is to try inhabiting the thing your theorems
295	quantify over with a trivial witness. Recording the probe next to the structure is what
296	stops the failure mode, because a named-but-vacuous input reads as progress.) -/
297	noncomputable def symPowDataTrivial (C : K) (n : ℕ) : SymPowData C n where
298	  carrier := ∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)
299	  proj := 𝟙 _
300	  desc := fun {_} h _ => ⟨h, Category.id_comp h, fun _ hu => by simpa using hu⟩
301	
302	omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
303	/-- **The other half of the witness: `symPowDataOne`'s projection is symmetric.**
304	
305	Every downstream theorem quantifies over a `SymPowData` *paired with* this hypothesis,
306	and the pairing is what rules out the trivial `proj := 𝟙` datum for `n ≥ 2`. Here it is
307	immediate: `Equiv.Perm (Fin 1)` is a subsingleton, so `σ 0 = 0` and `permAut_π` closes
308	it.
309	
310	Without this lemma the claim "the interface is inhabited" would not be machine-backed
311	end to end, since the bare structure is inhabited trivially. -/
312	theorem symPowDataOne_proj_perm (C : K) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin 1)) :
313	    MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ (symPowDataOne C).proj = (symPowDataOne C).proj := by
314	  have h : σ 0 = 0 := Subsingleton.elim _ _
315	  change MonObj.permAut C σ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0 = Pi.π (fun _ : Fin 1 => C) 0
316	  rw [MonObj.permAut_π, h]
317	
318	end CategoryTheory

preHom u f = u ≫ f := rfl

section PermAut

variable [HasFiniteProducts K]

/-- **The factor-permuting automorphism of `C^n`.** For `σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)`,
the morphism `C^n ⟶ C^n` whose `i`-th component is the `σ i`-th projection; on
points, `(P₁, …, P_n) ↦ (P_{σ 1}, …, P_{σ n})`. -/
noncomputable def permAut (C : K) {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) :=
  Pi.lift (fun i => Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) (σ i))

omit [CartesianMonoidalCategory K] in
@[reassoc (attr := simp)]
theorem permAut_π (C : K) {n : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) (i : Fin n) :
    permAut C σ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i = Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) (σ i) := by
  simp only [permAut, Pi.lift_π]

end PermAut

section PowSum

variable [HasFiniteProducts K] [BraidedCategory K]

/-- **The `n`-fold sum morphism `C^n ⟶ A`.** For `φ : C ⟶ A` into a commutative
group object, the morphism sending `(P₁, …, P_n) ↦ φ(P₁) * ⋯ * φ(P_n)`, formed as
the product in the commutative monoid `(C^n ⟶ A)` of the projections composed
with `φ`.

In the Albanese application `A` is an abelian variety and the group law is
written additively: this is `(P₁, …, P_g) ↦ φ(P₁) + ⋯ + φ(P_g)`. -/
noncomputable def powSum {C A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] (n : ℕ) (φ : C ⟶ A) :
    (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C)) ⟶ A :=
  ∏ i, (Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ)

/-- **Milne's "clearly this is symmetric".** The `n`-fold sum is invariant under
permuting the factors of `C^n`. The proof is exactly the commutativity of the
group law of `A`: in the *commutative* monoid `(C^n ⟶ A)` a finite product is
invariant under reindexing (`Equiv.prod_comp`).

This is the hypothesis consumed by the universal property of the symmetric power
`Sym^n C`, which is what licenses the factorisation `C^n ⟶ Sym^n C ⟶ A`. -/
theorem powSum_perm {C A : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] (n : ℕ) (φ : C ⟶ A)
    (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    permAut C σ ≫ powSum n φ = powSum n φ := by
  classical
  calc permAut C σ ≫ powSum n φ
      = ∏ i, (permAut C σ ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ) :=
        map_prod (preHom (permAut C σ)) _ Finset.univ
    _ = ∏ i, (Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) (σ i) ≫ φ) :=
        Finset.prod_congr rfl fun i _ => by rw [← Category.assoc, permAut_π]
    _ = ∏ i, (Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ) :=
        Equiv.prod_comp σ (fun i => Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ)

/-- `powSum` is natural in the source: precomposition distributes over the sum. -/
theorem comp_powSum {C A W : K} [MonObj A] [IsCommMonObj A] (n : ℕ) (φ : C ⟶ A)
    (u : W ⟶ (∏ᶜ (fun _ : Fin n => C))) :
    u ≫ powSum n φ = ∏ i, (u ≫ Pi.π (fun _ : Fin n => C) i ≫ φ) := by
  classical
  exact map_prod (preHom u) _ Finset.univ

end PowSum

end CategoryTheory.MonObj
